California is experiencing a homeowner’s insurance crisis. Many insurance companies have opted not to insure homes and have pulled out of California. Others now charge exorbitant rates placing stress on middle and lower income households. Housing insecurity is imminent for young families, senior citizens on fixed incomes, and people of color who are already struggling with the increased cost of living.

Although Insurance Commissioner Lara has been attempting to work with insurance companies, these companies, apparently, do not want take greater risks caused by wildfires and other climate events.

Mortgage companies require their borrowers to maintain homeowner’s insurance or risk being in default of their loans authorizing the lender to purchase insurance at cost to the borrower or foreclosure on the home. Borrowers unable to pay for the insurance will be forced to sell or suffer foreclosure. In my neighborhood, an insurance company (Farmer’s Insurance) raised homeowner insurance rates this year from twenty-two hundred dollars ($2,200) to eleven thousand dollars ($11,000) per year.

The solution to this problem is to statutorily preclude lenders from requiring mortgagees to obtain and maintain homeowner’s insurance. Homeowner’s insurance, for the most part, is to protect the lender. If the lender desires such protection, they should pay for it. The lender can insure the property for the mortgage balance and protect their interest or choose not insure it. The lender is making the money on these transactions and is in a better position to bear these costs to protect their interest. This would also be a business expense which should provide the lenders with tax advantages homeowners do not have. Lenders might also receive lesser rates by “bundling” the many properties on which they hold mortgages.

The same benefits will inure to renters. If a home lived in by the renter is subject to a mortgage and is subjected to these increased insurance rates, those increases will be reflected in higher rents. In many cases, the protections provided by the Tenant Protection Act of 2019 will not apply to these homes and the tenant may become homeless as rents continue to escalate. If the rental property is subjected to a foreclosure because the landlord is unable to pay the increased homeowner insurance amount, the property, again, may be subjected to foreclosure or sale causing the tenant to become displaced. Keep in mind that if a tenant is evicted, they will be subjected to any rental amount set by the new landlord. The result will be that families will be displaced.

Shifting the burden to the lender to insure their interest is the logical solution. This will maintain both homeowner and renter stability for California citizens.
